items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man woke unable to move his legs after a large carbohydrate-rich meal and heavy exercise the evening before. He has lost 4 kg in 2 months and has had palpitations. Temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse 124/min and blood pressure 146/70 mmHg. He has a fine tremor and a diffusely enlarged thyroid. Proximal leg strength is 1/5 with absent reflexes; sensation is normal. Serum potassium is 1.9 mEq/L, magnesium 1.9 mEq/L, phosphorus 2.1 mg/dL and bicarbonate 25 mEq/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and U waves. TSH is undetectable. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous potassium chloride at 40 mEq/h until the level is normal

options.label: B
options.html: Oral acetazolamide daily until strength returns

options.label: C
options.html: Oral propranolol with small doses of potassium

options.label: D
options.html: Oral spironolactone to cut renal potassium loss

items.explanationHtml:
Acute paralysis with severe hypokalemia, no acid-base disorder and thyrotoxicosis is thyrotoxic periodic paralysis. Thyroid hormone and catecholamines increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, and a carbohydrate load (insulin) shifts potassium into cells; total body potassium is normal. A nonselective beta blocker reverses the shift. Only small doses of potassium are given, with frequent levels, because rebound hyperkalemia is common as potassium leaves the cells. Definitive treatment of the hyperthyroidism prevents recurrence.

Takeaway: thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is a potassium shift: give propranolol and small potassium doses, and watch for rebound hyperkalemia.

whyNot.A: Rapid, large potassium replacement often overshoots into dangerous rebound hyperkalemia, because the potassium is in the cells, not lost.
whyNot.B: Acetazolamide helps some familial periodic paralyses but can worsen hypokalemia and is not used here.
whyNot.D: Spironolactone treats renal potassium wasting from mineralocorticoid excess, which is not the mechanism.
whyNot.E: Radioiodine treats the underlying Graves disease later; it does nothing for acute paralysis.

items.objective: Treat thyrotoxic periodic paralysis with a nonselective beta blocker and cautious potassium.
